Fixed-width windows as arrays for machine learning

Source: R/extract-windows.R
gextract.windows.Rd

Extracts fixed-width windows around a set of loci and returns their DNA as a one-hot array and the values of track expressions over them as a numeric array, ready to feed a sequence model. One call replaces gseq.extract, a one-hot encoding of the strings and gextract.matrix; the one-hot array is encoded in C++ straight from the sequence files.

Usage

gextract.windows(
  intervals = NULL,
  tracks = NULL,
  width = NULL,
  signal_width = width,
  jitter = 0,
  binsize = 1,
  use_strand = TRUE,
  exclude = NULL,
  min_counts = NULL,
  max_counts = NULL,
  count_track = 1,
  sequence = TRUE,
  dtype = c("raw", "integer", "double")
)

Arguments

intervals

the loci: 1D intervals (a data frame or the name of an intervals set), or a list of such, e.g. list(pos = peaks, neg = background), whose rows are concatenated and labelled by a 'set' column (the names of the list, or their indices)

tracks

track expressions (a character vector) for 'y', or NULL for sequence only. Its names, if any, name the second dimension of 'y'.

width

width of the sequence window

signal_width

width of the signal window

jitter

extra margin added to each side of both windows

binsize

bin size of the signals: a positive integer that divides signal_width + 2 * jitter. Each value is the one gextract.matrix returns for the bin (e.g. the mean of a dense track; use a virtual track with func = "sum" for sums).

use_strand

if TRUE, rows with strand -1 are reverse complemented (see Details)

exclude

intervals whose overlapping windows are dropped, or NULL

min_counts, max_counts

bounds on the sum of 'count_track' over the signal window (inclusive), or NULL

count_track

the track expression the count filters use: an index into 'tracks', or one of its names

sequence

if FALSE, 'x' is not computed (NULL)

dtype

storage type of 'x': "raw" (one byte per value, the default), "integer" or "double"

Value

A list with

x

the one-hot sequences, an array of dimensions c(N, 4, width + 2 * jitter) with channels A, C, G, T (see gseq.onehot), or NULL

y

the signals, a numeric array of dimensions c(N, T, (signal_width + 2 * jitter) / binsize), or NULL without 'tracks'

intervals

the kept rows, one per window, in their original order: 'chrom', 'start' and 'end' of the sequence window (jitter included), the 'strand' column if any, 'signal_start' and 'signal_end' with tracks, the other columns of 'intervals', 'index' (the row in 'intervals', 1-based) and, for a list, 'set'

dropped

the dropped rows: 'index' and 'reason'

Details

Each locus (a row of 'intervals') is centred at mid = start + (end - start) %/% 2. Its sequence window is [mid - width %/% 2 - jitter, mid - width %/% 2 + width + jitter) and its signal window is the same with signal_width: an odd width reaches one base further right than left. A positive jitter widens both windows by jitter on each side, so that a data loader can crop randomly shifted windows of the requested widths later without reading the genome again (as in tangermeme's extract_loci).

Rows are dropped, and listed in dropped with the first reason that applies, when

  • "off_chrom": the sequence window or (with tracks) the signal window runs past either end of the chromosome;

  • "excluded": either window overlaps an interval of 'exclude' (by at least one base; intervals of 'exclude' on chromosomes the genome does not have are ignored);

  • "min_counts" / "max_counts": the sum of the values of track expression 'count_track' over the signal window (as returned, i.e. after binning, NaN counted as 0) is below 'min_counts' or above 'max_counts'.

With use_strand = TRUE and a 'strand' column in 'intervals', the rows with strand -1 (or "-") are reverse complemented: their one-hot encoding is that of the reverse complement, and their signals are reversed along the length axis.

The arrays have the same axes as pymisha's gextract_windows: x[n, c, p] and y[n, t, b], i.e. (batch, channels, length). (R arrays are column-major, so the memory order differs from numpy's; indexing, and conversion to a torch tensor, are the same.)

Memory: 'x' takes N * 4 * (width + 2 * jitter) bytes with dtype = "raw" (4 and 8 times that for "integer" and "double"), and 'y' takes N * T * (signal_width + 2 * jitter) / binsize * 8 bytes for T track expressions. The signals are extracted with gextract.matrix in chunks of about 1e7 values, so the extraction itself adds little to that. For 100,000 windows of 2 kb, 'x' takes 800 MB; 'y' of three tracks at 1 bp resolution takes 4.8 GB, or 150 MB in 32 bp bins.

See also

gseq.onehot, gextract.matrix, gseq.extract

Examples


gdb.init_examples()
loci <- data.frame(chrom = "chr1", start = c(5000, 20000, 100), end = c(5001, 20001, 101))
w <- gextract.windows(loci, tracks = c(dense = "dense_track"), width = 500, binsize = 50)
dim(w$x)
#> [1]   2   4 500
dim(w$y)
#> [1]  2  1 10
w$dropped # the third locus is too close to the chromosome start
#>   index    reason
#> 1     3 off_chrom
